prime.problem: BatchNorm is the layer where hand-written gradients most often go wrong: its forward pass reuses tensors, broadcasts per-neuron statistics over the batch and sums over rows, and a gradient that forgets any of that is silently off.
prime.fits: You have dh from the matmul card. This card carries it back through tanh and BatchNorm's seven atoms to dhprebn, using the sum ↔ broadcast duality and the += rule for reused nodes from micrograd.
expect: tanh′ written with the output: 1 − h²
prime.goal: Write all twelve lines from dhpreact to dhprebn yourself, predict which cmp lines print False before a second branch is added, and say which rule each line uses.

attend: Why does Karpathy write tanh's local gradient with h instead of hpreact, and what does that save?
bngain has shape (1, 64) but dhpreact is (32, 64): which forward-pass operation forces a sum over rows in the backward pass?
Where does the 1/(n−1) in dbndiff2 come from, and what would change if BatchNorm used the biased 1/n variance?
Which two tensors feed more than one later operation, and how would you spot that by reading the forward code?
What is the difference between a tensor that is broadcast (needs a sum) and one that is used twice (needs +=)?

must: bndiff feeds both bnraw and bndiff2 → the loss depends on it through two paths → its gradient is the sum of both → one branch alone gives exact: False (maxdiff 0.00119) until dbndiff += adds the variance path; the same holds for hprebn via bndiff and bnmeani
A (1, 64) tensor (bngain, bnbias, bnvar_inv, bnmeani) is broadcast over 32 rows in the forward pass → it is reused 32 times → its gradient is the sum over rows, .sum(0)
A forward sum over rows (bnvar from bndiff2, bnmeani from hprebn) gives each row a slope of 1/(n−1) or 1/n → backward, every row gets the same broadcast share → dbndiff2 is dbnvar/31 in every row
tanh′(x) = 1 − tanh(x)² and h = tanh(hpreact) is already stored → dhpreact = (1 − h²) · dh needs no recomputation → saturated units (|h| near 1) pass back almost nothing
elevated: The mean branch adds the same dbnmeani/n to every row → it makes each column of dhprebn sum to about 0 (max 2.3e-9 here) → shifting all 32 inputs of a neuron by a constant can't change the loss, because BatchNorm subtracts the mean
reference: dbnmeani = (-dbndiff).sum(0) comes out (64,), not (1, 64); broadcasting still works
dhprebn = dbndiff.clone() before the +=, so the second branch doesn't modify dbndiff in place
the tensor names and shapes: hprebn, bnraw, hpreact, h are (32, 64); the statistics and bngain/bnbias are (1, 64)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the BatchNorm + tanh graph from hprebn to h, circle the two tensors that fan out, and next to every edge write the rule its backward line uses (slope, sum over rows, broadcast ÷ n, or +=).
checklist: tanh: multiply by 1 − h², using the stored output
γ, β, bnvar_inv and bnmeani were broadcast over rows, so their gradients are sums over rows
the variance and mean were sums over rows, so their gradients broadcast back, scaled by 1/(n−1) and 1/n
the power rule gives −½(bnvar + ε)<sup>−3/2</sup> for bnvar_inv
bndiff and hprebn each have two branches, so their gradients need +=
cmp after each line tells you exactly which line is wrong

retrieve.q: Explain why dbngain needs .sum(0, keepdim=True) but dbnraw doesn't, using the shapes of bngain, bnraw and dhpreact.
answer: bngain is (1, 64) and was broadcast to all 32 rows, so it is used 32 times and its gradient adds those 32 contributions
bnraw is (32, 64), the same shape as dhpreact, so each entry is used once: dbnraw = bngain * dhpreact elementwise
keepdim keeps (1, 64) so the gradient has the parameter's shape

retrieve.q: Walk the gradient from dbnvar_inv to the second share of dbndiff: name each local gradient and say which of them sums or broadcasts.
answer: power rule: dbnvar = −½(bnvar + ε)−3/2 · dbnvar_inv
bnvar was a sum of bndiff2 over rows ÷ (n−1), so dbndiff2 broadcasts dbnvar/(n−1) to every row
square: dbndiff += 2·bndiff · dbndiff2, added to the branch from bnraw

retrieve.q: You swap dbndiff += for dbndiff =. Which cmp lines fail, and why do the earlier ones still pass?
answer: everything up to bndiff2 is computed before that line, so it still passes
bndiff now holds only the variance branch, so it fails
bnmeani and hprebn are computed from dbndiff, so they inherit the error (measured maxdiffs 0.0083, 0.031, 0.0085)

retrieve.q: Twelve atomic lines vs Exercise 3's single-line BatchNorm backward: what do you gain and lose with each, and when would you pick the atomic version?
answer: atomic: every line is a known rule and cmp localises a bug to one line, but it's long and makes many temporary tensors
one line: compact, but a derivation slip is hard to find and it only matches to about 1e-9 (approximate, not exact)
pick atomic when checking or debugging, and use it as ground truth for the one-liner

compare.q: counts in the softmax chain and bndiff here both need +=. What is structurally the same about the two forward passes, and what is different about the axis they normalise over?
answer: same: a tensor is used directly and also through a statistic computed from itself (counts_sum; bnvar/bnmeani), so it has two branches
softmax normalises across the 27 columns of each row (sum over dim 1); BatchNorm normalises each column down the 32 rows (sum over dim 0)
so the broadcasts and sums run along different axes: keepdim on dim 1 there, dim 0 here
both fail the same way: one branch gives exact False

compare.q: The one-line dhprebn and this card's twelve lines compute the same gradient. What does the one-liner exploit that the atomic version doesn't, and how does each fail?
answer: the one-liner substitutes all the branches into one formula and simplifies (the mean's effect on the variance cancels)
it runs as a few broadcasted ops and matches to about 9.3e-10, not exactly
atomic version fails loudly and locally (one cmp line); the one-liner fails as a whole, with no hint which term is wrong

compare.q: micrograd's += bug and a missing dbndiff += are the same idea at different scales. Where does micrograd put the += for you, and why must you write it yourself here?
answer: micrograd's _backward closures always do self.grad +=, so any reused node accumulates automatically
here each gradient is a hand-written tensor line, so nothing accumulates unless you write += (and .clone() first)
same failure: the gradient reflects only the last branch written

predict.q: After the full backward pass, add up dhprebn down the batch for one neuron (a sum over the 32 rows). Before running it, what do you expect, and what would the sum be if you had skipped the bnmeani branch?
predict.answer: About 0: the largest column sum is 2.3e-9. Adding the same constant to all 32 inputs of a neuron shifts bnmeani by that constant too, so bndiff and the loss don't change; the gradient has no component along that direction. Without the mean branch, column 0 sums to −0.00547, exactly −dbnmeani[0]: the missing branch is precisely what cancels it.

apply.task: Break the lab two ways and predict each result before running. (a) Replace dbndiff += (2*bndiff) * dbndiff2 with =. (b) Restore it, then use 1.0/n instead of 1.0/(n-1) in dbndiff2. For each, name the first cmp line that fails, and say whether bnmeani survives.
apply.done: Your predictions match the run: (a) first failure bndiff (maxdiff 0.0083), and bnmeani fails (0.031); (b) first failure bndiff2 (7.7e-6), but bnmeani stays approximate: True (3.7e-9), and you can explain why.
apply.hint: In (b) the error only enters through the variance branch, 2·bndiff·dbndiff2, where dbndiff2 is the same in every row. What is the sum of bndiff down a column?
